Yes. I can open the **JusPrin v2** canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v), read any artboard, and publish changes back to it. It's the canvas `agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md` names as a source of truth, alongside the JusPrin Design System artifact, which is also listed in the canvas as its design system.

It has 212 artboards across 10 pages:

| Page | Artboards | What's on it |
|---|---|---|
| Main Page | 12 | Prepare first print, Home light/dark, chat list, printer popover, print timeline (including revert and dark versions) |
| Agent UI · States & Components | 18 | Tool and plan approvals, matrices for history, recovery, runtime, header, composer and messages, plus composer-redesign, model-menu and turn-activity proposals |
| Printer & Material Settings | 35 | Filament menus, slots and library, colour picker, printer menus, three add-printer steps, light and dark versions |
| Agent Setup · Empty State | 14 | API key entry, connect tool, prepare, review, save, error states |
| Design System | 46 | Buttons, fields, menus, chips, sheets, elevation swatches, composer, dialogs |
| Current Setup Card | 33 | Behaviour states, stress tests, All settings views, pinned docked band vs. floating card |
| Plates & Project Pane | 12 | 26a–26h plate and project rows, menus, print history |
| Onboarding | 33 | Screens 00–20 (welcome, sign-in, Orca import, first project, check print) plus delivery notes |
| Component Review (may not be needed) | 9 | System line, notice strip, code and diff blocks, tool strip, light and dark |
| Add Printer Flow (Obsolete) | — | — |

To work on it, I edit a board's source file and publish back to the same link. If someone has hand-edited that board in the meantime, the publish is refused and I redo my edit on their latest version, so their changes aren't overwritten.

What would you like changed? Give me the page and board names, or describe the screen, and I'll pull those boards up.

1	# JusPrin production documentation
2	
3	This directory is the canonical starting point for production work on `jusprin-newui`. It preserves the durable product and engineering decisions from `jusprin-v2-poc` without importing the POC's temporary windows, probes, static mocks, generated evidence, or environment-gated startup paths.
4	
5	Read these documents in order:
6	
7	1. [Product definition](product-definition.md) — the human/agent boundary, required product surfaces, workflow, and visibility rules.
8	2. [Production architecture](architecture.md) — the selected native/WebView architecture, ownership rules, component boundaries, and implementation sequence.
9	3. [Engineering and verification method](engineering-method.md) — how to assess risk and what evidence is required before calling a feature complete.
10	4. [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) — known Orca behaviors, lifecycle traps, event and history constraints, and testing lessons.
11	5. [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md) — required before changing any OrcaSlicer-owned file: where a seam belongs, why additive beats rewritten, how to leave a conflict that resolves correctly, and what evidence a change must record.
12	6. [Design system](design-system.md) — brand behavior, semantic UI tokens, typography, spacing, accessibility, and asset rules.
13	7. [POC reference](poc-reference.md) — exact pointers to the spike-only documents, code, commits, logs, screenshots, and generated brand artifacts left on `jusprin-v2-poc`.
14	8. [Tool extension guide](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md) — shared Agent/MCP contracts, process-settings workflow, execution and verification requirements.
15	9. [Local autosave and version history](autosave-version-history.md) — managed project storage, migration, restore, export, retention, and failure behavior.
16	
17	Printer UI without hardware (Bambu in-process fake; control file; isolated app): [Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md). Print-host (Klipper/Moonraker) simulation stays on `jusprin-newui-fakeprinter`.
18	
19	## Governing decisions
20	
21	- JusPrin is an AI-piloted 3D-printing product built on OrcaSlicer, not a replacement slicing engine.
22	- OrcaSlicer's C++ model, slicing pipeline, viewport, geometry operations, project serialization, and undo stack remain authoritative.
23	- The production application stays native C++/wxWidgets/OpenGL. The Agent conversation uses a local React/TypeScript application inside `wxWebView`.
24	- JavaScript renders state and submits typed commands; it never owns editable Orca project state.
25	- When logic could live in either C++ or a React page, it goes in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++: it touches Orca state, enforces a limit or boundary the app must guarantee, has to work without a page, or needs a thread or lifetime the page lacks. See [Where logic goes](architecture.md#where-logic-goes-the-page-first).
26	- Product policy lives in fork-owned files. OrcaSlicer-owned files receive only small, product-neutral, additive seams — every line changed there is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase.
27	- The user owns physical facts, object meaning, desired outcomes, privacy and legal decisions, and starting consequential physical actions.
28	- The production branch must not import experimental POC behavior merely because it demonstrated feasibility. Use the POC as evidence and reimplement through stable production boundaries.
29	
30	## Source lineage
31	
32	`jusprin-newui` and `jusprin-v2-poc` share base commit `8500fcdcca` (`v2.4.2`). The POC reference is pinned to final POC commit `9bba835b92`, so future changes to branch names do not make the historical evidence ambiguous.

1	# JusPrin product definition
2	
3	**Status:** Canonical product direction for the `jusprin-newui` production branch.
4	
5	**Source:** Consolidated from product discovery on `jusprin-v2-poc`. Historical inspection evidence remains on that branch; see [POC reference](poc-reference.md).
6	
7	## Executive summary
8	
9	An AI agent can remove much of a slicer’s technical complexity, but it cannot eliminate the need for user interaction.
10	
11	The boundary is:
12	
13	> The user tells the system what is physically true, what the object means, and what outcome is wanted. The agent chooses the technical printing strategy. The user verifies consequential decisions and remains in control of the physical machine.
14	
15	This produces three classes of OrcaSlicer features:
16	
17	1. **User-decision surfaces must remain prominent.**
18	   These capture information the agent cannot reliably obtain: physical setup, functional intent, geometry meaning, aesthetic preferences, legal restrictions, and control over real-world actions.
19	
20	2. **Shared agent-and-user surfaces should be redesigned.**
21	   The agent proposes a solution, explains it, and draws attention to uncertainty. The user reviews the result visually instead of manipulating dozens of parameters.
22	
23	3. **Implementation settings can disappear from the primary interface.**
24	   The agent can usually manage line widths, speeds, infill mechanics, cooling, retraction, support parameters, and similar technical details.
25	
26	The final product should therefore retain nine primary surfaces:
27	
28	1. Project knowledge
29	2. Physical setup
30	3. Print intent
31	4. Objects and plates
32	5. Essential geometry editing
33	6. Local meaning and overrides
34	7. Print-plan verification
35	8. Print preflight and live control
36	9. Calibration and troubleshooting
37	
38	These are not remnants of a legacy slicer. They are the information and control boundary between a person, an AI agent, and a physical manufacturing process.
39	
40	The interface should not give every retained feature equal weight. Features fall into four visibility levels:
41	
42	1. **Default** — continuously visible in an ordinary project.
43	2. **Contextual** — appears when the project, current selection, or agent uncertainty makes it relevant.
44	3. **On demand** — available through Project details, More, or the expert layer.
45	4. **Interruptive** — normally hidden, but made prominent when a consequential warning, mismatch, or unresolved decision occurs.
46	
47	Frequency alone does not determine visibility. A control can be rarely used but interruptive because overlooking it would be costly or unsafe.
48	
49	---
50	
51	# 1. Why an AI agent sometimes lacks enough information
52	
53	Before deciding which UI to retain, it helps to distinguish the different reasons an agent cannot safely make a decision.
54	
55	## 1.1 The agent cannot observe physical reality reliably
56	
57	A slicer may say that a particular nozzle, plate, or filament is selected, but that does not prove it is installed.
58	
59	Examples include:
60	
61	- The build plate was changed manually.
62	- The AMS contains a different spool than expected.
63	- Filament is wet, old, tangled, or nearly empty.
64	- A hardened nozzle was replaced with a standard nozzle.
65	- Glue was or was not applied.
66	- The print bed is occupied.
67	- A previous print remains attached to the plate.
68	
69	The agent can detect some of these conditions using printer sensors or a camera, but uncertainty must remain visible.
70	
71	## 1.2 The agent does not know what the geometry means
72	
73	A mesh contains shapes, not intentions.
74	
75	The agent may identify a hole, thin wall, flat face, or overhang, but it does not inherently know whether that feature is:
76	
77	- A precision bearing surface
78	- A screw hole
79	- A snap fit
80	- A decorative opening
81	- A sacrificial support
82	- A face that must remain smooth
83	- A surface hidden after assembly
84	- A region intended to flex
85	- A deliberately thin membrane
86	
87	This is why essential geometry editing and semantic annotation must remain.
88	
89	## 1.3 The agent does not know the user’s priorities
90	
91	There is rarely one objectively correct slicing strategy. A user may prioritize:
92	
93	- Appearance
94	- Strength
95	- Dimensional accuracy
96	- Speed
97	- Material savings
98	- Heat resistance
99	- Flexibility
100	- Watertightness
101	- Minimal support marks
102	- A particular color arrangement
103	
104	These priorities can conflict. The agent needs the user to define what “good” means.
105	
106	## 1.4 Some decisions are subjective
107	
108	Seam placement, surface texture, layer visibility, support scars, color boundaries, and acceptable print time are personal judgments.
109	
110	An agent can recommend an option, but it cannot determine the user’s taste from the model alone.
111	
112	## 1.5 Some actions have consequential real-world effects
113	
114	Starting a print consumes material, occupies a machine, creates heat and motion, and may run unattended for hours. Firmware updates and calibration changes can alter the behavior of the printer.
115	
116	The agent can prepare these actions, but the user needs final authority over them.
117	
118	## 1.6 Some information concerns ownership, law, or safety
119	
120	The agent cannot invent or silently change:
121	
122	- Authorship
123	- Licensing
124	- Commercial-use permission
125	- Safety warnings
126	- Assembly instructions
127	- Bill-of-materials information
128	- Intended use
129	- Privacy and cloud-connectivity preferences
130	
131	These are authoritative project facts, not slicing parameters.
132	
133	---
134	
135	# 2. The surfaces that must remain
136	
137	## 2.0 Project-window hierarchy
138	
139	The Project window should not treat Prepare, Preview, and Info as three equal destinations.
140	
141	- **Prepare is the dominant, persistent workspace.** It is where users inspect the model, communicate intent, manipulate geometry, resolve uncertainty, and review the agent's plan.
142	- **Check print opens Orca Preview in a modal window.** Prepare remains underneath; closing Check returns focus to Prepare. It is a secondary action when the active plate has a valid slice.
143	- **Info becomes Project details.** It is a drawer opened from the project name or menu. The agent reads its contents continuously even when the drawer is closed.
144	- **Print opens Send preflight.** It never sends directly. Explicit Send remains the consequential commitment.
145	
146	The normal flow is:
147	
148	`Prepare -> Check print -> return to Prepare if correction is needed -> Print -> Send preflight -> explicit Send`
149	
150	### Default Project-window composition
151	
152	The default window should contain:
153	
154	- Project name and saved/unsaved state
155	- Compact printer pointer: target printer, nozzle, build plate, and material
156	- Compact, editable intent summary
157	- Compact active plate/object summary
158	- 3D Prepare canvas
159	- Essential direct-manipulation tools
160	- Compact pinned agent plan
161	- Highest unresolved assumption, compromise, or risk
162	- Check print
163	- Print
164	- Consequential warnings when applicable
165	
166	The canvas is the primary human-agent collaboration surface. It must make the build plate and model visible, support camera rotation, pan, zoom, selection, and direct spatial manipulation, and show the changes the agent makes.
167	
168	The compact summaries should keep the governing assumptions visible without expanding full editors. Examples:
169	
170	> Decorative · appearance first · protect front surface · under 5 hours
171	
172	> Plate 1 · Fuzzy Heart · 1 copy · PLA Matte
173	
174	A one-object project should not permanently display a large object tree. A complete intent questionnaire should not remain expanded after it has been answered.
175	
176	### Direct resolution of uncertainty
177	
178	Warnings should link to the user action that resolves them rather than expecting the user to translate them into legacy slicer controls:
179	
180	- `Support enters this hole` -> `Protect this opening`
181	- `Seam crosses a visible face` -> `Mark visible face`
182	- `Strength direction is unclear` -> `Show load direction`
183	- `Part may not fit` -> `Enter critical dimension`
184	- `Support may be hard to remove` -> `Adjust supports`
185	
186	Each feature still has one authoritative home, but summaries, warnings, and resolution actions may appear elsewhere. For example, Printer Configuration owns the installed hardware state while Prepare shows a compact pointer and any mismatch.
187	
188	## 2.1 Project knowledge
189	
190	This surface answers: **What is this project, and what does someone need to know about it?**
191	
192	OrcaSlicer exposes model descriptions, creator information, pictures, license information, profile notes, accessories, bills of materials, assembly guides, and other attachments.
193	
194	A project inspected during product discovery contained a safety instruction limiting it to electric tea lights. That information could affect how the agent evaluates material, temperature exposure, and intended use.
195	
196	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
197	
198	The mesh does not contain reliable authorship, licensing, safety, assembly, or use-case information. An agent may extract clues, but it must not treat guesses as project facts.
199	
200	### What should remain
201	
202	- Project name and saved/unsaved state
203	- Project description
204	- Author and license
205	- Safety and usage instructions
206	- Reference pictures
207	- Assembly instructions
208	- Bill of materials and accessories
209	- Important profile notes
210	- Project save, version, backup, and ownership controls
211	
212	### What the agent should do
213	
214	The agent should read this material before planning the print, highlight contradictions, and ask about missing safety or assembly information when relevant.
215	
216	Only the project name and saved/unsaved state need to remain in the normal Project-window chrome. The rest belongs in the Project details drawer and surfaces automatically only when consequential:
217	
218	- Safety or usage warning: on import, when it affects planning, and before Print
219	- License restriction: when sharing, publishing, using commercially, or exporting
220	- Assembly instructions: for multi-part projects and plate organization
221	- Bill of materials or accessories: when non-printed components are required
222	- Reference image: when it clarifies orientation, color, or intended appearance
223	- Profile note: when the agent proposes deviating from it
224	- Recovery or version warning: when work is unsaved or versions conflict
225	
226	The user should not have to open Project details for its contents to influence the plan.
227	
228	---
229	
230	## 2.2 Physical printer setup
231	
232	This surface answers: **What hardware and material will actually perform the print?**
233	
234	### What should remain
235	
236	- Target printer
237	- Nozzle diameter and nozzle type
238	- Build-plate type
239	- Loaded filament and material
240	- Filament color
241	- AMS or multi-material slot mapping
242	- Printer availability and current condition
243	- Important mismatches between configuration and observed hardware
244	
245	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
246	
247	Configured state and physical state can diverge. Selecting “PLA” in software does not establish that PLA is actually loaded, dry, correctly mapped, or compatible with the installed plate and nozzle.
248	
249	### What the agent should do
250	
251	- Discover printers and materials automatically
252	- Read AMS and printer state where available
253	- Compare observed state with the project
254	- Recommend compatible profiles
255	- Explain mismatches
256	- Ask the user only about unresolved physical facts
257	
258	The existing setup wizard’s enormous lists of printer and filament profiles should become hardware discovery followed by a short confirmation.
259	
260	---
261	
262	## 2.3 Print intent
263	
264	This surface answers: **What outcome does the user want?**
265	
266	Instead of beginning with hundreds of process parameters, the product should ask for meaningful requirements.
267	
268	### What should remain
269	
270	- Intended use
271	- Visual versus functional priority
272	- Strength direction
273	- Accuracy requirements
274	- Important dimensions or clearances
275	- Heat, chemical, outdoor, food-contact, or flexibility requirements
276	- Desired surface quality
277	- Maximum acceptable print time
278	- Material or color requirements
279	- Acceptable and unacceptable support contact
280	- Whether this is a prototype or final part
281	
282	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
283	
284	The same model can legitimately be printed with different orientations, materials, wall structures, infill, supports, and tolerances depending on its purpose.
285	
286	A decorative prototype and a load-bearing final component may use identical geometry but require completely different plans.
287	
288	### What the agent should do
289	
290	Translate intent into technical settings. For example:
291	
292	> “This is a visible decorative object, so I oriented it to protect the front surface, moved the seam to the rear, and accepted a longer print to reduce visible layer artifacts.”
293	
294	The user should judge that reasoning without having to configure every underlying value.
295	
296	The full intent editor should appear during project creation, import, or when requirements are incomplete. Afterward, Prepare should retain only a compact editable summary. Specialized questions such as food contact, flexibility, critical clearances, and protected support surfaces should appear contextually rather than in every project.
297	
298	---
299	
300	## 2.4 Objects, parts, and plates
301	
302	This surface answers: **What exactly is included in this job?**
303	
304	OrcaSlicer’s object and plate tree is essential, although its presentation can be simplified.
305	
306	### What should remain
307	
308	- Every plate in the project
309	- Every object and part
310	- Object names
311	- Quantity and duplicates
312	- Which objects are enabled
313	- Which material or extruder each object uses
314	- Modifiers, support enforcers, and support blockers
315	- Object-specific requirements
316	- Print order where it matters
317	- Search for complex projects
318	
319	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
320	
321	The agent cannot assume that every imported object should be printed or that apparently duplicated parts are accidental. A modifier may encode engineering intent that is invisible in the rendered outer surface.
322	
323	Multi-plate organization can also represent batches, material differences, alternative versions, or assembly groups.
324	
325	### What the agent should do
326	
327	Arrange objects, detect accidental overlaps, identify likely duplicates, balance plates, and suggest grouping—but show the resulting job manifest for confirmation.
328	
329	For a simple one-object, one-material, one-plate project, show a compact job summary by default. Expand the full object-and-part tree contextually when the project contains multiple objects, parts, plates, materials, modifiers, or print-order constraints. Search should appear only when the project is complex enough to need it.
330	
331	---
332	
333	## 2.5 Essential geometry editing
334	
335	This surface answers: **Does the printable geometry need to be intentionally changed?**
336	
337	This was underrepresented in the previous report. Geometry editing must remain a first-class capability.
338	
339	### Default operations
340	
341	- Add and remove models
342	- Select parts
343	- Move, rotate, and scale
344	- Place a model on a chosen face
345	- Arrange models on the plate
346	- Duplicate and change quantity
347	- Undo and redo
348	
349	### Contextual operations
350	
351	These remain first-class capabilities but should appear under More, through the selected-object menu, or when the situation calls for them:
352	
353	- Mirror
354	- Cut and split
355	- Merge or assemble related parts
356	- Add text or labels
357	- Measure dimensions and clearances
358	- Work with multiple plates
359	- Repair or identify problematic geometry
360	- Create intentional modifiers
361	- Paint supports, seams, materials, or other region-specific behavior
362	
363	Examples of contextual surfacing include offering Cut for an oversized model, Measure when fit or clearance matters, Repair when mesh defects are detected, and region annotation when the agent cannot determine where support contact is acceptable.
364	
365	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
366	
367	Changing geometry can change the object’s meaning.
368	
369	The agent cannot safely assume that it may:
370	
371	- Cut a model into pieces
372	- Fill or enlarge a hole
373	- Change scale
374	- Move two components relative to one another
375	- Mirror an asymmetric part
376	- Emboss text
377	- Remove an apparently unnecessary detail
378	- Reorient an assembly
379	- Create a different mating surface
380	
381	Even when a change improves printability, it may make the part unusable.
382	
383	### What the agent should do
384	
385	The agent may propose geometry changes and generate previews:
386	
387	> “Splitting the model here eliminates most supports and hides the joint on the rear surface.”
388	
389	But the user should review meaning-changing operations. Direct manipulation must remain available because communicating spatial corrections in words is often slower than moving or painting them on the model.
390	
391	---
392	
393	## 2.6 Local meaning and region-level overrides
394	
395	This surface answers: **Are different parts or surfaces subject to different requirements?**
396	
397	Global instructions such as “make it strong” are often insufficient.
398	
399	### What should remain
400	
401	Users need ways to identify:
402	
403	- Faces that must remain smooth
404	- Surfaces where support contact is allowed or forbidden
405	- Precision holes and mating surfaces
406	- Areas requiring additional strength
407	- Flexible or sacrificial regions
408	- Visible versus hidden faces
409	- Preferred or forbidden seam locations
410	- Different material or color regions
411	- Areas where texture is intentional
412	- Object-specific print requirements
413	
414	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
415	
416	Computer vision can estimate geometry, but it cannot reliably know the functional role of every region.
417	
418	For example, an agent may place a seam on the geometrically least visible face, unaware that the face mates with another part. It may strengthen the thickest region even though failure occurs around a small mounting hole.
419	
420	### What the agent should do
421	
422	Use semantic labels to generate modifiers and technical settings automatically. Users should describe meaning; they should not normally need to configure local speeds, wall counts, or infill percentages themselves.
423	
424	---
425	
426	## 2.7 Agent print plan
427	
428	This surface answers: **What strategy has the agent chosen, and why?**
429	
430	This is the AI-first replacement for most of OrcaSlicer’s process-setting panels.
431	
432	### What should be shown by default
433	
434	- Selected orientation
435	- Overall material, strength, support, and surface-quality strategy
436	- Most important assumption the agent could not verify
437	- Most important compromise or unresolved risk
438	
439	### What should appear when expanded
440	
441	- Detailed rationale and alternative plans
442	- Confidence by decision
443	- Important deviations from the normal printer profile
444	- Full change history
445	- Numerical implementation settings through the expert layer
446	
447	### Why this surface is needed
448	
449	Even when the agent has enough information to choose technical values, hiding its entire plan would make errors difficult to recognize.
450	
451	The user may not need to know that a particular wall speed is 72 mm/s, but they should know that the plan emphasizes surface quality over speed.
452	
453	### What the agent can normally control
454	
455	- Layer-height strategy
456	- Line widths
457	- Wall and top/bottom structure
458	- Infill density and pattern
459	- Speeds and acceleration
460	- Cooling and temperature within qualified ranges
461	- Retraction and wiping
462	- Bridge behavior
463	- Support style, density, and interface parameters
464	- Brim, skirt, priming, and adhesion aids
465	- Purging and flushing calculations
466	- Seam implementation after the user states the preferred region
467	- Printer-specific G-code from a trusted profile
468	
469	These settings should remain accessible to experts, but they do not need to be primary beginner-facing surfaces.
470	
471	Do not always show time and material estimates in Prepare. Show them there only after a valid background slice exists. Until then, the plan can say `Ready to check`.
472	
473	---
474	
475	## 2.8 Check print: print-plan verification
476	
477	This surface answers: **What will the printer actually do?**
478	
479	OrcaSlicer’s Preview capability is not merely an expert visualization. It is the last opportunity to discover a bad plan before material and machine time are consumed. **Check print** opens the current valid slice in a modal window using Orca's real Preview widget and G-code renderer. The window closes if that slice or its project changes. For now, Print stays the primary action for every valid slice and Check print stays in its menu; agent findings do not change that action.
480	
481	### Default verification
482	
483	- Overall appearance of the sliced result
484	- Estimated time
485	- Material usage and cost
486	- Highest-priority warnings
487	- Comparison with the user’s stated intent
488	
489	When supports exist, support verification becomes the default Check view:
490	
491	- Support locations
492	- Contact surfaces and likely scars
493	- Supports that may be difficult to remove
494	- Supports entering holes, cavities, or mating regions
495	- A direct Adjust supports or Mark protected areas action that returns to Prepare
496	
497	If no supports exist, Check should emphasize the most consequential detected risk instead.
498	
499	### Contextual verification
500	
501	- Seams on protected or visible surfaces
502	- Risky bridges and overhangs
503	- Thin or missing features
504	- First-layer contact problems
505	- Unsupported islands
506	- Unexpected gaps or collisions
507	- Material or color changes
508	- Purge volume and waste
509	- Prime tower and extruder assignments
510	
511	### Expert verification
512	
513	OrcaSlicer’s more detailed views should remain available on demand:
514	
515	- Line type
516	- Layer height
517	- Line width
518	- Speed
519	- Fan speed
520	- Temperature
521	- Volumetric flow
522	- Layer time
523	- Extruder assignment
524	- Layer-by-layer playback
525	- Individual toolpath playback
526	- Visibility toggles for walls, infill, bridges, supports, travel, retraction, wiping, and seams
527	- Raw G-code inspection
528	
529	### Why the agent cannot independently verify its own plan
530	
531	The preview is produced from the same assumptions and algorithms that created the plan. It is evidence, but it is not independent knowledge of the user’s intent.
532	
533	An agent may verify that a toolpath is internally consistent while still misunderstanding which surface must remain smooth or which opening must stay unobstructed.
534	
535	### What the agent should do
536	
537	Inspect the complete preview automatically and present a short risk-focused report. The user should review the meaningful consequences instead of manually examining every toolpath by default.
538	
539	Layer count and the complete extrusion-role legend are not beginner decision aids. Keep them in Inspect toolpaths with the other expert diagnostics.
540	
541	---
542	
543	## 2.9 Print preflight
544	
545	This surface answers: **Is the correct job about to be sent to the correct physical machine?**
546	
547	Prepare should contain a visible Print entry point. Print opens this preflight; it does not bypass it:
548	
549	`Print -> Send preflight -> explicit Send`
550	
551	The current Print action opens Orca's existing Select Machine or printer-host send dialog, which requires a separate send/upload choice. The complete JusPrin preflight checklist below remains future product work.
552	
553	### What should remain
554	
555	- Job name and thumbnail
556	- Destination printer
557	- Selected plate
558	- Time and material estimate
559	- Filament and AMS mapping
560	- Plate-type confirmation
561	- Bed-leveling choice
562	- Flow-calibration choice
563	- Timelapse choice
564	- First-layer inspection
565	- Build-plate detection
566	- Tangle and clumping detection
567	- AI-monitoring behavior and sensitivity
568	- Recovery options
569	- Warnings about disabled checks
570	- Explicit Send control
571	
572	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
573	
574	This is where digital assumptions become a real physical operation. The chosen printer may be occupied, prepared with another plate, located remotely, or loaded with valuable material.
575	
576	Some monitoring options also involve privacy, camera use, false-positive tolerance, or printer-specific limitations.
577	
578	### What the agent should do
579	
580	Perform the preflight, recommend safe defaults, and block obviously inconsistent jobs. The user should see a concise checklist and start the send themselves.
581	
582	---
583	
584	## 2.10 Live printing and device control
585	
586	This surface answers: **What is happening now, and can the user intervene?**
587	
588	OrcaSlicer’s Device surface demonstrates that an AI slicer is also partly a printer-control product.
589	
590	### What should remain immediately accessible
591	
592	- Camera
593	- Job progress
594	- Current layer and remaining time
595	- Printer state
596	- Nozzle and bed temperatures
597	- Important fan or light controls
598	- Health and fault alerts
599	- Pause
600	- Resume
601	- Stop
602	
603	Manual movement, homing, detailed fan control, storage, and file management can be contextual or expert functions.
604	
605	### Why the agent cannot control this invisibly
606	
607	Sensors and vision systems can be wrong. Users may notice a sound, smell, obstruction, detaching part, or safety concern that the system cannot observe.
608	
609	Pause and stop are human override mechanisms. They should never be hidden inside a conversation or require the agent’s cooperation.
610	
611	### What the agent should do
612	
613	Monitor the job, explain anomalies, recommend intervention, and automatically pause only under rules the user set in advance. It should clearly report why an automatic intervention occurred.
614	
615	---
616	
617	## 2.11 Calibration and troubleshooting
618	
619	This surface answers: **Is the printer-material combination behaving as expected?**
620	
621	The audit found both guided calibration pages and more advanced generators.
622	
623	### Relevant calibration capabilities
624	
625	- Flow dynamics
626	- Flow rate
627	- Temperature
628	- Pressure advance
629	- Retraction
630	- Maximum volumetric speed
631	- VFA
632	- Junction deviation
633	- Input-shaping frequency and damping
634	
635	### Why the agent cannot completely own calibration
636	
637	Calibration depends on physical evidence:
638	
639	- Filament may be wet.
640	- Adhesion may be poor.
641	- Transparent or reflective filament may confuse optical sensors.
642	- A nozzle may be worn or partially obstructed.
643	- A user may judge two samples differently.
644	- Automatic measurements contain uncertainty.
645	- An apparently better surface may reduce strength or accuracy elsewhere.
646	
647	### What the agent should do
648	
649	The agent should:
650	
651	1. Diagnose the observed symptom.
652	2. Decide whether calibration is justified.
653	3. Select the appropriate test.
654	4. Choose safe test ranges.
655	5. Explain what to observe.
656	6. Analyze sensor data or photographs.
657	7. Recommend a result.
658	8. Say what was saved to the printer or filament profile and that it can be changed back.
659	
660	The user should not be presented with every calibration parameter unless manual control is requested.
661

664	## 2.12 Privacy, updates, portability, and expert administration
665	
666	These functions are used less frequently, but they are important for particular users and organizations.
667	
668	### User-owned decisions
669	
670	- Cloud login region
671	- Stealth or offline mode
672	- Network-plugin use
673	- Preset synchronization
674	- Multi-device management
675	- Firmware and application update timing
676	- Camera and monitoring privacy
677	- Backup and recovery policy
678	- Importing and replacing configurations
679	- Ownership and export of project data
680	
681	### Capabilities that should remain available
682	
683	- Import 3MF, STL, STEP, SVG, OBJ, AMF, ZIP archives, and configurations
684	- Export models, projects, sliced plates, G-code, and preset bundles
685	- Export printer, filament, and process profiles
686	- Manage downloaded and stored printer files
687	- Access timelapses
688	- Run network diagnostics
689	- Open configuration data
690	- Enable developer tools

692	### Why the agent cannot decide these alone
693	
694	These choices affect privacy, compatibility, organizational policy, intellectual property, and the user’s ability to leave the product.
695	
696	The agent can simplify the workflows, but it should not silently enable cloud communication, install firmware, replace profiles, or trap projects in a proprietary format.

699	
700	# 3. Recommended final product structure
701	
702	The application should use one main window rather than turning every stage of a print into equal global navigation.
703	
704	## 3.1 Home
705	
706	Home is the hub for:
707	
708	- Printer cards showing availability, condition, and loaded filament
709	- Project gallery, open, and project status
710	- Import of 3MF, STL, STEP, SVG, OBJ, AMF, and ZIP files
711	- Entry to project versions and backups
712	- Launching Monitor
713	
714	## 3.2 Project window
715	
716	The Project window contains the print-planning lifecycle without dividing it into equal destinations:
717	
718	- **Prepare:** dominant workspace containing intent, objects and plates, the 3D canvas, geometry editing, local meaning, and the agent plan
719	- **Check print:** temporary sliced-verification mode
720	- **Project details:** drawer for authoritative project knowledge
721	- **Print:** entry point to Send preflight
722	
723	Prepare may point to Printer Configuration, but it does not own machine calibration, filament inventory, maintenance, or privacy settings.
724	
725	## 3.3 Printer Configuration
726	
727	Printer Configuration owns:
728	
729	- Target printer, nozzle, and build-plate configuration
730	- Loaded filament, material colors, AMS, and multi-material inventory
731	- Calibration workflows
732	- Troubleshooting and maintenance
733	- Firmware-update timing
734	- Camera and monitoring privacy
735	- Network plugins and diagnostic tools
736	- Stored printer files and timelapses
737	
738	Prepare displays a compact pointer to this state and surfaces mismatches; it does not duplicate the complete configuration UI.
739	
740	## 3.4 Monitor
741	
742	Monitor is a pop-out surface so it can remain visible while the user works elsewhere. It owns:
743	
744	- Camera
745	- Progress, current layer, and remaining time
746	- Printer state
747	- Nozzle and bed temperatures
748	- Health and fault alerts
749	- Pause, Resume, and Stop as never-hidden human overrides
750	
751	Manual movement, homing, detailed fan or light control, storage, and file management are contextual.
752	
753	## 3.5 Overlays and application-level layers
754	
755	- **Send preflight:** final job, destination, material mapping, safety, and monitoring confirmation followed by explicit Send
756	- **Expert layer:** raw process settings, numeric per-object and per-region overrides, manual calibration ranges, toolpath diagnostics, and G-code
757	- **Preferences:** cloud region, stealth/offline behavior, network plugins, sync, updates, privacy, backup and recovery, import/export administration, and developer tools
758	
759	This structure preserves the lifecycle of a print without turning Setup, Intent, Plan, Verify, Print, Monitor, and Diagnose into nine equal screens.
760

764	
765	## 4.1 Default
766	
767	Continuously visible in the ordinary Project window:
768	
769	- Project name and saved/unsaved state
770	- Current printer, nozzle, plate, and material summary
771	- Compact intent summary
772	- Compact active plate and object summary
773	- 3D Prepare canvas
774	- Add, remove, select, move, rotate, scale, place on face, arrange, duplicate, Undo, and Redo
775	- Compact agent plan
776	- Highest unresolved assumption or risk
777	- Check print and Print
778	
779	Inside Check, the default changes to sliced appearance, time, material, cost, the highest-priority warning, and comparison with intent. When supports exist, support placement and removal risk become the default Check emphasis.
780	
781	## 4.2 Contextual
782	
783	Shown when the project or current task makes it relevant:
784	
785	- Full object, part, and plate tree
786	- Per-object material or extruder
787	- Modifiers, support enforcers, blockers, print order, and search
788	- Local surface annotations and object-specific requirements
789	- Mirror, cut, split, merge, assemble, text, measure, repair, positive/negative parts, and multi-plate distribution
790	- Seam, bridge, overhang, thin-feature, first-layer, island, and collision inspection
791	- Material changes, purge waste, prime tower, and extruder assignments
792	- Time and material estimate in Prepare after a valid background slice exists
793	- Assembly instructions, accessories, and reference pictures
794	- Calibration and maintenance recommendations
795	- Firmware updates, storage, timelapses, and multi-device management
796	
797	## 4.3 On demand
798	
799	Available through Project details, More, or the expert layer:
800	
801	- Full intent questionnaire after it has been completed
802	- Project description, author, license, pictures, BOM, assembly guide, and profile notes
803	- Version, backup, ownership, and export administration
804	- Detailed agent rationale, alternatives, confidence, profile deviations, and change history
805	- Individual speeds and accelerations
806	- Exact line widths
807	- Infill and support implementation parameters
808	- Retraction, wiping, cooling, and purge details
809	- Complete toolpath legend and playback
810	- Raw G-code
811	- Manual calibration ranges
812	- Network tests, configuration folders, developer mode, and visualization preferences
813	
814	## 4.4 Interruptive
815	
816	Normally hidden, but presented prominently at the point where the user can resolve it:
817	
818	- Wrong printer, nozzle, plate, or filament
819	- Safety or usage instruction relevant to the current plan
820	- Unsupported, missing, or defective geometry
821	- Support entering a protected region
822	- Violated dimensional requirement
823	- Material incompatible with the stated use
824	- Agent uncertainty about a meaning-changing geometry operation
825	- License conflict during sharing, publishing, commercial use, or export
826	- Unsaved work, recovery issue, or version conflict
827	- Printer-health or safety alert
828	
829	---
830	
831	# 5. The final design rule
832	
833	For every OrcaSlicer control, ask four questions:
834	
835	1. **Does this require physical information the software may not possess?**
836	   Keep a user confirmation surface.
837	
838	2. **Does this depend on the object’s purpose, meaning, or the user’s taste?**
839	   Keep an intent, annotation, or direct-editing surface.
840	
841	3. **Does this start a consequential, legal, private, or physical action?**
842	   Keep explicit user control.
843	
844	4. **Is this merely a technical method for achieving an already-understood goal?**
845	   Let the agent manage it and expose it only when explanation or expert control is needed.
846	
847	That rule preserves the genuinely human parts of OrcaSlicer while allowing the agent to remove most of its parameter complexity.
848

1	# JusPrin production architecture
2	
3	**Status:** This is the architecture chosen for the `jusprin-newui` branch. It also says where production code may and may not reach into OrcaSlicer.
4	
5	JusPrin replaces what OrcaSlicer looks like and how people move through it. It keeps everything OrcaSlicer already does well to turn a model into a print. Product work should make it easier for people to say what they want and to check a print before sending it. It must not create JusPrin's own version of slicing, geometry, rendering, picking (working out which object the pointer is on), saving and loading, or undo history.
6	
7	## Product composition
8	
9	The project window we are building toward has four regions that stay in place:
10	
11	1. A compact row that shows the printer and the project status.
12	2. A thin pane that lists plates and objects and can be collapsed.
13	3. OrcaSlicer's existing Prepare canvas (the 3D view).
14	4. A fixed pane that holds the Agent conversation and the print plan.
15	
16	The compact plates/objects pane is deferred to a later task. The first
17	production shell and the first Agent implementation must not depend on it.
18	Until the pane is added, people work with objects through the native canvas
19	and the Agent.
20	
21	Prepare is the screen people stay on. **Check print** opens a modal window. That window holds a second copy of OrcaSlicer's real Preview widget and shows the current valid slice of the active plate. OrcaSlicer's original Preview stays where it was, in `Plater`'s Notebook (OrcaSlicer's tabbed container). A small factory function on `Plater`, with nothing JusPrin-specific in it, gives that window the existing model, bed, slicing process, and G-code result. Closing the window returns focus to Prepare. The window also closes by itself when the project or the slice changes. **Print** currently opens OrcaSlicer's existing send confirmation dialog. It never sends straight away. Project details open as a drawer. Monitor is a separate screen that can stay visible while the person does other work.
22	
23	## Runtime architecture
24	
25	```text
26	OrcaSlicer process (C++17 / wxWidgets / OpenGL)
27	├── JusPrin application shell
28	│   ├── compact top navigation and machine status
29	│   ├── native plates/objects pane
30	│   ├── center workspace host
31	│   │   └── existing GLCanvas3D Prepare canvas
32	│   └── wxWebView
33	│       └── local React/TypeScript Agent interface
34	├── modal Check print window with Orca G-code Preview
35	├── typed workspace/controller boundary
36	├── existing Orca model, selection, plates, gizmos, and undo stack
37	└── existing slicing, project I/O, device, and print subsystems
38	```
39	
40	The split between native code and web code is deliberately cautious:
41	
42	- The 3D view, and anything drawn on top of it, stays native.
43	- The top row and the object/plate pane start as native wxWidgets.
44	- C++ owns the application state and the project state.
45	- The WebView receives versioned events and sends versioned commands.
46	- We may later try building the object pane in a WebView, but only as a change to how that one pane is drawn. It would not be a reason to move to Electron or to a WebGL 3D view.
47	
48	## Authoritative ownership
49	
50	For each kind of state, one part of the system holds the real copy. This table says which part, and what JusPrin does with that state.
51	
52	| Concern | Authoritative owner | JusPrin responsibility |
53	|---|---|---|
54	| Project model and object identity | Orca `Model` and `ObjectID` | Show a typed view that is valid only for the current project session |
55	| Plates and active plate | Orca `PartPlateList` | Show them, and ask for changes through commands |
56	| Selection and picking | Orca `Selection` and `GLCanvas3D` | Keep the UI in sync without creating feedback loops |
57	| Geometry transforms | Orca gizmos and `GizmoObjectManipulation` | Start the existing behavior and show exact values |
58	| Undo and redo | Orca undo stack | Report whether undo and redo are available and what they did. Keep no second undo stack |
59	| Slicing and Preview | Orca slicing actions and Preview canvas | Show the states of Slice and Check print |
60	| Project serialization | Orca 3MF and model serializers | Keep files compatible. Add migration only for new data |
61	| Agent conversation | React/TypeScript WebView | Render messages, write the words people and the model read, and submit typed commands (see [Where logic goes](#where-logic-goes-the-page-first)) |
62	| Agent print plan | C++/agent application boundary | Explain intent, decisions, uncertainty, and consequences |
63	
64	## Production integration boundaries
65	
66	### Shell host
67	
68	The shell is the JusPrin window frame around OrcaSlicer's content. Build one shell, in files this fork owns, and attach it to `MainFrame` in one small place. Decisions about what happens at startup go in a bootstrap or a shell factory that the fork owns. Do not spread environment checks through OrcaSlicer's constructors.
69	
70	The first production version may still construct OrcaSlicer's old top bar, tab panel, Sidebar, and `GUI_ObjectList` where existing OrcaSlicer behavior depends on them. Leave them out of the visible layout. Do not hide them behind a separate top-level window. Stopping them from being constructed at all is a separate project, because it changes object lifetimes.
71	
72	### Build registration
73	
74	List JusPrin's source files explicitly in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/sources.cmake`. OrcaSlicer's central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt` should pull that file in with one include line that never changes. The fork should not keep adding its own files to OrcaSlicer's list.
75	
76	### Workspace boundary
77	
78	The workspace API is the typed C++ interface JusPrin uses to read and change the project. The production version should keep the ideas from the proof of concept (POC) that worked:
79	
80	- separate types for plate IDs and object IDs, so one cannot be passed where the other is expected;
81	- read-only snapshots of the project;
82	- explicit errors from commands;
83	- typed reasons that say what kind of change happened;
84	- a revision number that only goes up;
85	- subscriptions that end automatically when the object holding them is destroyed, and that can be moved but not copied.
86	
87	Before production use, the API must also:
88	
89	- say which calls must run on the GUI thread;
90	- say exactly when the revision number goes up;

1	# JusPrin design system
2	
3	**Status:** Canonical product and brand guidance for `jusprin-newui`.
4	
5	JusPrin should make advanced 3D printing feel immediate: a confident path from model to machine that removes detours without hiding control. The product should feel focused, assured, inventive, and approachable. Its voice is direct, capable, and optimistic—never cute, cryptic, or over-engineered.
6	
7	The original JusPrin logo was supplied by the user and restored from repository revision `6eecb78b19`. The purple gradient endpoints were verified from the source SVG. Positioning language in the POC brand kit is proposed product direction, not an externally sourced market claim.
8	
9	## Brand behavior
10	
11	- **Focused:** every element earns its place.
12	- **Assured:** guidance is calm and actions are decisive.
13	- **Inventive:** the product is technical without being intimidating.
14	- **Approachable:** use plain language instead of slicer jargon where possible.
15	- Make the next action obvious. Brand behavior should feel as focused as the visual system.
16	
17	The logo suggests an end-to-end journey through its orbit, precision and momentum through the crossing diagonals, flexible control through the open circle, and technical confidence softened by warmth through the purple gradient.
18	
19	Write the name exactly as **JusPrin**: capital J and P, no space, never all caps in body copy. Use surrounding text color for the name in ordinary copy; do not force a gradient into small text.
20	
21	## Logo use
22	
23	The primary expressions are the horizontal lockup, the compact product mark, and the text wordmark. Use the compact mark for application icons and small product contexts.
24	
25	- Clear space: at least one quarter of the mark width on every side.
26	- Minimum digital mark: 24 px.
27	- Minimum digital horizontal lockup: 120 px.
28	- Minimum printed mark: 8 mm.
29	- Minimum printed lockup: 32 mm.
30	- Below these sizes, use the mark alone and verify that the orbit arcs remain distinct.
31	
32	Always use the original artwork, preserve its aspect ratio and components, maintain clear space, and place it on White, Mist, Ink, or another quiet solid field. Do not stretch, rotate, redraw, arbitrarily recolor, outline, shadow, separate, or place it directly over visual noise. Monochrome is allowed only when required. If the center crossing or orbit loses clarity, increase size, contrast, or space.
33	
34	## Brand palette
35	
36	| Name | Value | Use |
37	|---|---:|---|
38	| Orbit | `#3A2D64` | Primary brand color and decisive light-mode action |
39	| Violet | `#6F4F84` | Secondary brand color, headings, and essential boundaries |
40	| Bloom | `#CE84B7` | Expressive accent and dark-mode primary action |
41	| Ink | `#17131F` | Primary text and dark canvas |
42	| Mist | `#F6F2F7` | Soft canvas and grouped surfaces |
43	| Trace | `#E8DFEB` | Light dividers and quiet structure |
44	| White | `#FFFFFF` | Primary light canvas |
45	| Success | `#2D6A55` | Light success state |
46	| Danger | `#B44757` | Light error or destructive state |
47	| Warning | `#D49A2A` | Light warning state |
48	
49	The signature gradient runs from Orbit to Bloom. Reserve it for the original logo, splash, onboarding, and rare hero moments. Do not use it as ordinary product chrome.
50	
51	Product code must resolve colors through semantic tokens in `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`; raw palette values are not a component API.
52	
53	## Semantic color behavior
54	
55	Dark mode is a semantic remapping, not a visual inversion. Preserve hierarchy, density, and geometry while choosing the dark value for the same named intent.
56	
57	Core mappings include:
58	
59	| Token | Light | Dark | Purpose |
60	|---|---:|---:|---|
61	| `surface.canvas` | `#FFFFFF` | `#17131F` | Main application background |
62	| `surface.subtle` | `#F6F2F7` | `#211B2A` | Sidebars and grouped settings |
63	| `surface.raised` | `#FFFFFF` | `#2B2336` | Dialogs, menus, elevated panels |
64	| `surface.raisedHover` | `#F6F2F7` | `#3B3047` | The hovered or keyboard-focused row in a menu or popover |
65	| `text.primary` | `#17131F` | `#F6F2F7` | Headings, values, body copy |
66	| `text.secondary` | `#5F5767` | `#CFC5D3` | Descriptions and secondary labels |
67	| `border.subtle` | `#E8DFEB` | `#4B3E57` | Dividers and quiet structure |
68	| `border.strong` | `#6F4F84` | `#7D6A8D` | Focus and essential boundaries |
69	| `action.primary` | `#3A2D64` | `#CE84B7` | Decisive primary action |
70	| `action.primary.hover` | `#4B3A77` | `#D99AC5` | Pointer hover |
71	| `action.primary.pressed` | `#2B214F` | `#B76CA0` | Pressed or active state |
72	
73	The JSON token file is authoritative for the code and contains the complete action, status, selected-surface, disabled, text, and component values. Every colour it shares with the design system holds the design system's value; `tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp` pins each one beside its design-system name. Secondary and danger buttons have no colours of their own: like the design system's Button/Secondary they have no fill, a `border.subtle` (secondary) or `status.danger` (danger) stroke, and `text.primary` or `status.danger` text, with `surface.subtle` on hover and `surface.selected` when pressed. `overlay.scrim` and `status.successOnAction` exist only in the code until the Design System artifact adds them.
74	
75	## Typography
76	
77	Product UI uses fonts already shipped by OrcaSlicer:
78	
79	- HarmonyOS Sans SC Regular for body and controls.
80	- HarmonyOS Sans SC Bold for hierarchy and actions.

I read the `agent-docs` index, the [JusPrin README](jusprin/README.md), the whole [product definition](jusprin/product-definition.md), and the opening sections of the [architecture](jusprin/architecture.md) and [design system](jusprin/design-system.md) docs. Here is the goal of the fork as I understand it.

## What JusPrin is

JusPrin is OrcaSlicer with an AI agent doing most of the technical work. It does not replace OrcaSlicer's slicing engine. OrcaSlicer still handles the model, slicing, the 3D view, geometry tools, saving files and undo. JusPrin changes how the app looks and how people move through it.

The main idea is a split of responsibilities:

> The person says what is physically true, what the object is for, and what result they want. The agent picks the printing strategy. The person checks the important decisions and stays in control of the printer.

## How that changes the slicer

Every OrcaSlicer control goes into one of three groups:

1. **Things only the person can know stay prominent.** This covers what is really loaded in the printer, what a part is for, which faces must stay smooth, how long a print can take, and licence or safety notes.
2. **Shared screens get redesigned.** The agent proposes a plan and explains it, and the person reviews the result visually instead of adjusting dozens of settings.
3. **Technical settings leave the main screen.** Speeds, line widths, infill, cooling, retraction and support details are the agent's job. Experts can still reach them.

The test for any control is four questions:
- Does it need physical facts the software can't see?
- Does it depend on what the object means or on the person's taste?
- Does it start something consequential, like a print?
- Or is it just a technical way to reach a goal that is already clear?

Only the last kind is handed to the agent.

## The product it's aiming for

- **Home**: printer cards, a project gallery, file import, and a way into Monitor.
- **Project window**: Prepare is the screen people stay on. It has a compact printer and material row, a short summary of the person's goals, the plate and object list, OrcaSlicer's 3D canvas, and the Agent pane with its pinned plan and the top risk it hasn't resolved.
  - **Check print** opens OrcaSlicer's real Preview in a modal window.
  - **Print** opens a send check (preflight) and never sends on its own. The person always presses Send.
  - **Project details** is a drawer for licence, safety notes, assembly instructions and similar facts. The agent reads it even when it's closed.
- **Printer Configuration**, a pop-out **Monitor** where Pause and Stop are never hidden, calibration guided by the agent, and an expert layer for raw settings.

Not every control gets the same weight. Some are always visible, some appear only when relevant, some are reachable on request, and some interrupt only when ignoring them would be costly.

## How it's built

- The app stays native C++/wxWidgets. The 3D view stays native too.
- The Agent conversation is a React page inside a WebView. It shows state and sends typed commands, but it never holds the real project data.
- JusPrin's product decisions live in its own files. Changes to OrcaSlicer's files must be small and added on rather than rewritten, because each one has to be redone whenever upstream changes are merged in.
- The look comes from the brand palette (Orbit purple, Bloom pink, Ink, Mist), applied through named tokens. The two Claude artifacts, the Design System and the JusPrin v2 canvas, are the source of truth for it.

## How this connects to the canvas

The JusPrin v2 canvas pages match the product definition fairly directly:
- **Main Page** covers Home and Prepare.
- **Current Setup Card** is the pinned plan.
- **Plates & Project Pane** is the plate and object list.
- **Printer & Material Settings** is the printer and material row.
- **Agent UI** and **Agent Setup** are the conversation pane.
- **Onboarding** is first launch through to a first print.

content.text:
# Adapting OrcaSlicer's Preferences for JusPrin: brainstorm

I haven't changed anything in the code or on the canvas.

## What OrcaSlicer has today

OrcaSlicer's Preferences window has 6 tabs and about 75 settings, all shown with equal weight:

| Tab | What's in it |
|---|---|
| **General** | Language, units, which page opens first, dark mode, one window at a time, splash screen, downloads folder. Also project load behaviour, auto backup, recent files, a few save/export options, preset grouping, multi-device management |
| **Control** | Auto flush, auto arrange, auto slice, the mixed-temperature limit, camera and mouse controls, "clear my choice" resets |
| **Graphics** | Realistic view, anti-aliasing, frame-rate limit |
| **Online** | Login region, stealth mode, Bambu Cloud, network test, updates and preset sync, the network plug-in |
| **Associate** (Windows only) | Which file types and web links open in the app |
| **Developer** | Developer mode, log level, experimental options, debug |

JusPrin has never modified this dialog: `Preferences.cpp` is identical to the v2.4.2 base commit. JusPrin's only link to it is the "Preferences…" item in the project overflow menu, which opens OrcaSlicer's dialog unchanged ([StatusRow.cpp:541](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/StatusRow.cpp:541)).

## Gaps this leaves in JusPrin

1. **There is nowhere to manage the Agent after setup.** The app tells people to *"Add it in the Agent settings"* ([AgentHost.cpp:3163](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentHost.cpp:3163)). The design-system doc also says providers are added "from the Agent settings". That place doesn't exist, so there is no way to change, add or remove a key.
2. **App-level notices have no home.** These are app updates, plug-in updates, profile updates and sync conflicts. [NoticeKinds.cpp:82](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrintIssues/NoticeKinds.cpp:82) says they belong "on Home or in Preferences … and that place does not exist."
3. **There is nowhere to see or manage the account.** The onboarding boards on the canvas sign people in with Google or an email code. Nothing shows "signed in as …" or offers sign out afterwards.
4. **Some OrcaSlicer settings mislead in JusPrin.**
   - "Auto backup" does nothing while JusPrin's version history is on, because the shell suspends it.
   - "Default page", "Hide login side panel", "Optimize filaments area height" and "Group user filament presets" all control OrcaSlicer screens that JusPrin hides.
   - The wording says "OrcaSlicer" throughout.
5. **It contradicts the product definition.** Section 3.5 gives Preferences a clear job: things the person decides, like cloud region, offline mode, plug-ins, sync, updates, privacy, backup, import/export and developer tools. Section 4 says technical details should be reachable on request, not given equal weight.

## Sorting the settings

I used the same four questions the product definition uses for every OrcaSlicer control.

- **The person's decision, so keep it prominent:**
  - Language, units, light/dark theme.
  - Camera and mouse behaviour.
  - Login region, stealth/offline mode, Bambu Cloud, network plug-in.
  - Update and sync choices.
  - File and link associations, downloads folder.
- **New in JusPrin:**
  - Account.
  - Agent: providers and keys, default model and thinking level.
  - Privacy: what the AI provider gets to see.
  - Version history: what is kept, where it lives, how much space it uses.
  - Switch to classic view, which currently sits in the project menu.
- **Handled by the agent, or replaced by JusPrin, so leave them off the main list:**
  - Auto flush, remember printer configuration, filament grouping and area height, shared-profile notices, the filament grouping pop-up.
  - Auto backup, which version history replaces.
  - Default page, the login side panel, recent-file count.
- **For experts, reachable on request:**
  - All of Graphics and all of Developer.
  - Draco export quality, full source paths, keep painting after mesh changes.
  - Abnormal storage, skip the AMS blacklist, show unsupported presets.
  - The mixed-temperature limit. This one is a safety guard, so it belongs here, not hidden away.
  - "Clear my choice", which could become one "Reset dismissed questions" button.

## Three ways to build it

**A. Keep OrcaSlicer's dialog and only recolour it.** This is what happens today. It costs nothing at rebase time, but it fixes none of the gaps above.

**B. Change OrcaSlicer's dialog by hiding settings and adding JusPrin tabs.** I'd avoid this. All the settings are built in one very long function in a 2,200-line file that upstream edits often. Every hidden setting would be another conflict to resolve at each rebase, which goes against the fork-stewardship rules.

**C. A JusPrin-owned Preferences window (my recommendation).** It would live in fork-owned files and have a short list of sections. It would read and write the same saved settings, so classic view and JusPrin always agree. At the bottom, "All OrcaSlicer preferences…" would open the upstream dialog unchanged. That dialog can already open on a chosen tab, so linking straight to Graphics or Developer needs no change to OrcaSlicer.

The catch with C is that some settings do more than save a value when OrcaSlicer's dialog closes:
- A language change rebuilds the whole window.
- A dark-mode change redraws every screen.
- On Windows, file associations are written to the system.
- Graphics changes redraw the 3D view.

C must call the same OrcaSlicer functions, not copy them. The cleanest way may be one small additive change to OrcaSlicer: move that after-close work into a function JusPrin can call. The simpler alternative is to leave the settings with these side effects in OrcaSlicer's dialog for now.

C could be drawn natively or as a React page like Home and the Agent. Page-first points to React: the Agent key-entry screens already exist there and could be reused, and the design tokens come for free. C++ would still own reading and writing the settings.

## A possible layout for C

1. **Account:** who is signed in, sign out.
2. **Agent:** providers and keys (add, replace, check, remove), default model and thinking, what the agent can see, redo setup.
3. **Printers & cloud:** region, offline mode, Bambu Cloud, network plug-in, network test.
4. **Appearance:** language, units, theme.
5. **3D view:** camera style, zoom, mouse actions, plus a "Graphics quality…" link to OrcaSlicer's tab.
6. **Projects & files:** version history, downloads folder, file and link associations.
7. **Updates:** app, built-in profiles, preset sync. This would also be the home for the update notices.
8. **Advanced:** switch to classic view, reset dismissed questions, open the configuration folder, log level, "All OrcaSlicer preferences…".

Entry points would be the project overflow menu (already there), a gear on Home, and the standard app menu / Cmd+, on macOS.

## Questions for you

1. **Is a JusPrin account definitely coming?** The onboarding boards assume one. If so, Account goes at the top. If not, Agent does.
2. **Window or Home view?** It could be its own window like OrcaSlicer's, or a full-page view inside Home.
3. **Should OrcaSlicer's dialog keep showing everything?** That includes settings JusPrin replaces, like Auto backup. Hiding them there would mean changing OrcaSlicer's file, which I'd avoid unless they cause real confusion.
4. **What about "Auto slice after changes"?** The product definition shows time and material estimates only after a valid background slice. Should JusPrin decide this itself rather than leave it as a preference?

Once you've picked a direction, the next step would be a new "Preferences" page on the JusPrin v2 canvas. The canvas has no Preferences boards yet.

Here's the plan updated with your answers.

**What changes**
- **Bambu Cloud and everything tied to it is hidden.** That covers the Bambu Cloud switch, login region, the network plug-in setting, network test, cloud preset sync, encrypted token storage and multi-device management. Printer setup already installs it when a printer needs it (`OrcaPrinterBackend::install_network_plugin`), so it doesn't need a setting. I'd also hide stealth mode, since all it does is turn off Orca's and Bambu's cloud. If JusPrin later wants an "offline" switch, it would mean something different (no account, no AI), so it would be designed as a new setting.
- **No expert options.**
- **A link to OrcaSlicer's dialog.** A small "OrcaSlicer preferences…" link at the bottom of the page opens it unchanged, for anyone who needs the rest.

**Where it opens.** You're right that a view inside Home won't work: it would make people leave Prepare. The most intuitive option is a separate window that opens on top of whatever screen you're on:
- It opens from a gear in the header on both Home and Prepare, from the project menu item that exists today, and from Ctrl+, / Cmd+,.
- Sections are listed on the left and their settings on the right.
- Changes take effect immediately, with no OK/Cancel. The exception is language, which says it will reload the window before it applies.
- I'd keep the name **Preferences** rather than "Settings", because "All settings" already means print settings in the setup card.

**Sections**
1. **Account:** who is signed in, sign out.
2. **Agent:** providers and keys (add, replace, check, remove), default model and thinking level, what the agent can see, redo setup.
3. **Appearance:** language, units, dark mode.
4. **3D view:** camera style, zoom to mouse, reverse zoom, mouse-button actions, free camera.
5. **Projects & files:** version history, downloads folder, and on Windows, which files and links open in JusPrin.
6. **Updates:** stable releases only, update built-in printer profiles. This is also where app-update notices would live.

Give every artboard whose content really works (handlers, inputs, navigation) `"is_interactive": true` in its canvas.json entry — only those get the blue mark and a Play button; leave it off static comps. A clickable prototype is one artboard per screen, joined by links (Links between artboards, below). A PAGE (landing page, dashboard, web app screen, scrolling explainer) gets `"expand": "fill"` on its artboard entry and a fluid root — in the full-window view it fills the window and scrolls as a page (without `fill` it is shrunk to fit); side menu + content: a `flex-wrap: wrap` row, content `flex: 999 1 560px; min-width: 0`, so the menu (never sticky or `100vh`) stacks on a phone; toolbars wrap; wide tables get an `overflow-x: auto` box; a one-file design can launch focused (`{"launch": {"view": "focused", "file": "Main.dc.html"}}`). - LAYOUT GUIDES: an artboard entry may carry `"guides"`, up to 6, drawn by the canvas OVER the artboard, never in Play, exports or markup: `{"kind":"columns","count":12,"gutter":24,"margin":80}` (align `"stretch"`, default, divides the width inside `margin`; `"start"|"center"|"end"` pack `count` tracks of `"size"` px, `"offset"` in from that edge; `"count":"auto"` = as many as fit), `{"kind":"rows",…}` (same fields down the height; default `"auto"` 8 px rows every 8), `{"kind":"grid","size":8}`; any may add `"color"` (hex or rgb()/hsl(), alpha = strength; default red at 10%) and `"hidden":true`. Always set the `hint-*` attrs (they render while values stream in). - **Links between artboards**: `<a href="Cart.dc.html">View cart</a>` moves Play to that artboard, in place or full window (not while editing). The href is the target's path relative to this artboard's; a leading `/` means the canvas root (`/sub/Cart.dc.html`). Style the `<a>` itself as the button: a `<button>` or input inside it swallows the click. `href="#id"` scrolls within the artboard; `https://…` opens a tab. Each artboard keeps its own `state`, so a flow that must share state across screens is ONE artboard: its handlers set a `state` field, `renderVals()` returns one flag per screen from it, and each screen sits in its own `<sc-if>`. - **Conditional styling in a loop**: precompute the varying piece per item in `renderVals()` (e.g. each item carries `ringStyle` or `selected`) and either branch with `<sc-if>` or bind the computed value — a style hole is acceptable for live, state-driven values (selection highlights) and for a declared tweak prop (`{{accent}}`), just never for other static theme tokens, which belong inline so they paint while streaming. - **Logic class**: plain classic JS, no TypeScript, no import/export; must be `class Component extends DCLogic`. result.output:
# Local autosave and version history

JusPrin saves authored projects in the application data directory under
`jusprin/projects/<project-id>/`. The project ID is independent of the source
filename. Opening an external 3MF or model imports it into a managed draft;
autosave never overwrites the source. **Saved** means the printable
project checkpoint and the current JusPrin document are durable. A 3MF is written
to a user-selected path only through **Export project 3MF…**. A copied 3MF does
not include local versions, conversations, or attachments.

The project header's actions menu exposes the save state, version history,
recent local projects, and export. Version history restores an earlier model
and its effective project settings. The native window title shows the managed
project name and the same save state as the header. Orca's dirty asterisk
does not represent whether the local project has been saved. Before restoring,
JusPrin saves and pins
the current version, then records the restore as a new version, so the prior
state remains available. Each older timestamp has a separate Restore button;
clicking the timestamp does nothing, and Restore asks for confirmation. A blank authored project gets one empty baseline
version so it can be reopened; later document edits do not add versions. A
first Agent model operation pins that baseline as its before-version.
Conversations with each chat's intent and plan, audit, and completed print
records remain in the current document; restoring a model marks the active
chat's plan for reassessment. Region descriptions follow the model: each
version records the list it was saved with, and restoring it brings that list
back. Restoring a model does not undo physical prints or change
global printer facts. Agent
mutations save and pin their actual
before-state, then link an after-version and outcome in an operation record.

## Storage and recovery contract

The restoration rules above describe ordinary Version history. **Restore and
resume** is a separate chat transition. Each chat owns its print intent and
plan; the project's current ones are the active chat's. A chat's checkpoint
holds a model-version reference and a structured setup summary of the moment
it was left. Browsing an older chat does not change the working project.
Resuming it saves and pins the outgoing state, restores the model with its
region descriptions, and activates that chat, whose intent and plan never left
it, only after the new document is durable. Other conversations, audit and print
records, and global printer facts remain. This does not add a full project-
document copy to model versions or make document edits create model versions.
Ordinary Version history remains model-only and does not activate an older
chat. An interrupted chat transition leaves a durable pending marker and
blocks that managed project for explicit recovery on restart.

I've added a new **Preferences** page to the [JusPrin v2 canvas](https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v). I haven't opened the canvas to look at the result, because the canvas's rules say not to check renders unless you ask. Tell me if you want me to go through it.

The page has 12 boards in three rows:

- **One board per section:** Account, Agent, Appearance, 3D view, Projects & files and Updates. The first board can be clicked through in Play: switch sections, sign out and back in, open the add-key field, and flip Light/Dark to see the whole window change.
- **States:** signed out, adding an OpenAI key, a new version available, and Agent in dark mode.
- **Where it opens:**
  - The window over Prepare, so you can see it isn't a Home-only view.
  - A board with the four ways in: the gear already on Home, "Preferences…" in a project's ⋯ menu, Ctrl+, (⌘, on Mac), and "Add a key…" links in the Agent.

The OrcaSlicer link is a small "OrcaSlicer preferences…" at the bottom of the left-hand list, so it shows on every section. Every board uses the same window file, so a change there shows on all 12.

There is no Bambu Cloud, region, stealth mode, network plug-in, cloud sync or anything for experts. A note at the top of the page records these decisions.

**Assumptions I made, so you can correct them:**
- **The JusPrin account provides the Agent's AI.** I based this on the "Continue with JusPrin · Free account" option on the Agent setup boards. The Agent section shows the account alongside Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenRouter keys, plus the AI tools on this computer, such as Claude Code.
- **MakerWorld stays.** I kept the option for "Open in slicer" buttons on Printables, MakerWorld and Thingiverse. MakerWorld is Bambu's model site, not their cloud. Say if you'd rather drop it.
- **No new gear in Prepare.** Prepare opens it from the ⋯ menu and the shortcut, without adding a button to its top bar.
- **Placeholders:** the version number and the last-checked time are left as [VERSION] and [TIME].

The auto-slice question is still running in [Decide how JusPrin handles auto-slice](#local_ac606645-e5c4-4125-a689-7896a5b8072a).

Another session was adding a Calibration page to the canvas at the same time. I published only my own boards and added my entries to the shared index, so that work is untouched.

content.text:
The auto-slice session recommends that JusPrin slice the active plate by itself about two seconds after the last change. It would wait while someone is mid-edit or the Agent is mid-turn, and it would need no change to OrcaSlicer's files. No code was changed. Its notes are in [auto-slice-findings.md](C:\Users\guitest\AppData\Roaming\Claude\side-session-notes\local_626ee175-7819-464c-a97e-9269b2eefe7e\auto-slice-findings.md).

It also found that OrcaSlicer's "Auto slice after changes" already does nothing inside JusPrin. It only runs while OrcaSlicer's Preview tab is showing, and JusPrin hides that tab. So leaving it off the new Preferences window takes nothing away from anyone.

Building this would touch several existing pieces:
- **Chat cards:** today every slice opens a "Slicing plate N" card in the chat, which would be noisy if slicing runs on its own.
- **Slice warnings:** the Agent's print-issues check reacts to new slice warnings, whoever started the slice.
- **Code comments:** several assume JusPrin never slices in the background.

Details are in [its session](#local_ac606645-e5c4-4125-a689-7896a5b8072a).
